open.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: Mind the flat. It's got nails in it and so have I. Maureen Keel, stage manager, and if you're the Americans you can hold this end.
Twice nightly, a matinee Tuesday, and the pier moves under you when the tide's in. You get used to it. You get used to anything down here.
She said 'you get used to anything' to the flat, not to us.

passives.line: Three layers of pins on the call board, and the bottom layer holds something older than the rest. Nobody pins over a thing they mean to throw away.
She looked at the change booth on her way in. She looks at it every morning, and she has never once gone over.

options.text: We'll hold it. Tell us about the summer seasons.
Nails in the flat and nails in you. Which came first?
(Take the end of the flat and say nothing.)

season.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: Twenty-two of them. Comics, sopranos, a dog act, a man who ate glass. The camp sends its lot over on Tuesdays, always has, for the coach parties.
You strike it all on the Tuesday night and you build it again Wednesday. Twenty-two years. The sea's the only set that stays up.
She counts the years like a woman who's counted them before, dear.

wry.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: The flat. The flat always comes first. That's the job.
Ha. All right. You can stay. Most people who come backstage want a photo with the cardboard sea.

silent.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: You've done this before. Or you've stood still before. Same muscles. Right, it's up, ask your questions.

hub.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
hub.prompt: Go on. The matinee's at two and I've a cyc to drop.
lines: Go on. The matinee's at two and I've a cyc to drop.

static.line: The cyc is still back there. The sea with the mud on it. She's stood in front of it every day for twenty-one years. Make her turn round.

options.text: You struck that big set every Tuesday in '73. Who built it?
There's something under the pins on your call board. Older than the rest.

fail.line: There's twenty years of pins on that board. You'll find a bus timetable and a dead moth. Leave it.

options.text: Colin described a wall of dials with the sea behind it. He described your set, Maureen. Say it.
Sunny Jim. Off the camp rota on the 29th. He did your Tuesday matinee. Where did he go after?
We'll let you get the cyc down.

builder.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: Himself. The lad in the act. Three nights in our scene dock with a borrowed jigsaw and the camp's paint, and he sang while he did it. Mouth-organ in the breaks.
Lovely hands. Rotten carpenter. The flats never sat square and the dials were painted on with a kitchen brush, and from row F it was the best thing I ever lit.
He built the dials himself. So the dials are his, not the camp's.

builder_fail.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: The camp built it. The camp builds everything and sends us the bill for the nails.
Ask Terry Gosling at Sunnyside. He signed for it. He signed for a lot that year.

pins.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: ...You can photograph it. You can't have it. It's held that board up since before you were shaving.
Don't move the top pins. Just the corner. There. Halfway down the bill. Don't read it out loud, the walls are hardboard.
A programme. 1973. A novelty act, by arrangement with the holiday camp.

confess.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: ...Flats painted with dials. Floor to flies. A cyc behind with the sea on it, lit from the back so it looked like a window. From the stalls you'd swear.
It went back to the camp in September and the cyc had marsh mud on the bottom foot of it. I wrote RETURNED DAMAGED. I didn't write where the mud came from.
He described my set. For ten pence a go, twenty-one years, and I sold him his first pint in '82 and never said a word.
She's put it down now. You can see it in her shoulders.

shut.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: Say it. Say it, she says. In my own dock, with the matinee at two.
I've nothing to say and a cyc to drop. Pass door's that way. Mind the nails.
She didn't say no. She said she'd nothing to say. Different thing, and we've lost the day on it.

jim.speaker: sf_stage_mgr
lines: Sunny Jim. Nobody's said that name to me since the second comic went to Blackpool.
He didn't go anywhere after the pier. That's the thing. He did the Tuesday matinee and he was on the Ryde train the next morning, Terry said, and nobody saw him on it.
He left his mouth-organ in my dock. I've still got it. It's in the drawer under the board with the fuses, and I've never played it.
A man leaves his instrument and his hat and his set. He didn't leave. He was left.
